documents.title: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

chunks.content: Graphical abstract INTRODUCTION Pheochromocytomas, which are now categorized as adrenal paragangliomas (PPGL) and PPGL are rare neuroendocrine tumors arising from the adrenal medulla and the paraganglia of the autonomic nervous system, respectively, with diverse clinical behaviors ranging from benign to highly aggressive forms [ - ]. Accurate prognostication remains a challenge due to the heterogeneous nature of these tumors and the lack of universally accepted histopathological grading systems [ - ]. The Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal Gland Scaled Score (PASS) has been proposed to stratify the risk of malignancy and adverse clinical outcomes [ , ]. However, limitations such as inter-observer variability and inconsistent predictive performance have been reported, raising concerns about its clinical utility [ - ]. The PASS, originally developed by Thompson, incorporates multiple histopathological parameters but lacks quantitative standards for each, leading to variability in interpretation and application across institutions [ , - ]. Previous research has demonstrated that the PASS, despite its modest overall performance, maintains a high negative predictive value (NPV), suggesting a potential role as a screening tool [ , - ]. Given these challenges, there is a need to refine prognostic models for PPGL to improve reproducibility and predictive accuracy. Recent efforts to develop a simplified scoring system, focusing on key histopathological features with the strongest associations to adverse events, have shown promise in reducing inter-observer variability and enhancing prognostic performance [ , , - ]. This multicenter study aims to evaluate the prognostic significance of the PASS across five tertiary referral centers in Korea, assess inter-institutional variability, and validate the utility of simplified PASS scoring systems for risk stratification in PPGL patients. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study cohort and data collection Five tertiary referral centers in Korea participated in this multi center study investigating the prognostic factors for paragangliomas. The participating institutions were Seoul National University Hospital (SNUH), Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (SNUBH), Samsung Medical Center (SMC), Seoul St. Mary’s Hospital, and Severance Hospital. All data were fully anonymized and merged prior to analysis, so that investigators were blinded to the identity of the contributing institutions. A total of 1,523 patients diagnosed with PPGL from 2007 to 2020 in 5 hospitals were initially identified. Among these, three cases of gangliocytic paraganglioma and two cases of cauda equina paraganglioma were excluded from the cohort, as these entities are currently classified as composite gangliocytoma/neuroma and neuroendocrine tumor, and cauda equina neuroendocrine tumor, respectively, according to the latest World Health Organization (WHO) classification of endocrine and neuroendocrine tumors [ ]. Therefore, the final study cohort comprised 1,518 patients. Of the total cohort, PASS information was available in 1,079 cases. Definition of clinical outcomes Adverse events were defined as the presence of recurrence, metastasis, or multifocality. Recurrence was defined as tumor relapsing in the vicinity of the operative bed. Metastasis was defined as pathologically or radiologically confirmed tumor spread to sites outside the operative bed, specifically bone and lymph nodes [ , - ]. Multifocality was defined as the presence of additional tumors, excluding bone or lymph node, detected at the time of pathological diagnosis. Recurrence-free survival (RFS) was defined as the interval from the date of surgery to the most recent follow-up or the time when an adverse event occurred. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed using R Software (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Continuous variables were compared using analysis of variance (ANOVA), and categorical variables were analyzed with Fisher’s exact test. Survival outcomes were evaluated with Kaplan-Meier plots and the log-rank test in the subset of 363 cases with available RFS data. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess prognostic factors for RFS in these 363 cases. For adverse event outcomes, univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted separately for patients with available PASS data (n = 1,079). Pair-wise Delong test was performed for comparison of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) among five institutes. A two-sided p-value < .05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS Baseline characteristics The baseline characteristics of the study cohort are summarized in . Mean age, sex distribution, tumor size, tumor localization, PASS, and disease status are presented for each hospital. Significant differences in mean age were observed among the institutes (ANOVA, p < .05); specifically, hospital D had a higher mean age compared to hospitals A and E. PASS also differed significantly among groups, with hospital A exhibiting higher scores than the other hospitals. For tumor localization, cases of paraganglioma in which the localization could not be identified in the electronic medical records were classified as unknown. PASS as prognostic indicator of adverse events Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the odds ratios of each variable in the total cohort of 1,518 cases ( ). In univariable analysis, all variables except sex were statistically significant. However, in multivariable analysis, only age (per 10 years) (odds ratio [OR], 0.68; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.60 to 0.76; p < .001) and PASS category (intermediate risk [4–5]: OR, 2.05; 95% CI, 1.22 to 3.35; high risk (≥6): OR, 4.83; 95% CI, 3.12 to 7.50; p < .001) remained significant. Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were conducted for the 363 cases with available survival data. Survival curves were stratified by age (≤45 years vs. >45 years), sex, tumor localization (adrenal vs. extra-adrenal), tumor size (≤5.0 cm vs. >5.0 cm), and PASS category (low risk [≤3], intermediate risk [4–5], high risk [≥6]), as shown in . According to the log-rank test, significant differences in survival were observed for age and PASS score categories (all p < .001). In contrast, sex, tumor localization, and tumor size did not show statistically significant differences in survival. Cox proportional hazards regression analysis for disease-free survival indicated that all variables except sex were statistically significant in univariable analysis ( ). In multivariable analysis, age (per 10 years) (hazard ratio [HR], 0.71; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.83; p < .001), localization (extra-adrenal: HR, 2.96; 95% CI, 1.71 to 5.14; p < .001), and PASS category (intermediate risk [4–5]: HR, 6.12; 95% CI, 2.3 to 16.3; high risk [≥6]: HR, 12.5; 95% CI, 5.49 to 28.5; p < .001) remained significant. Both multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards analyses demonstrated the prognostic significance of histopathological grading systems. The screening role of PASS: high NPV offsets modest predictive performance The predictive performance of the PASS score for adverse events was further evaluated using logistic regression-based receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, as summarized in . The PASS demonstrated an AUC of 0.673, sensitivity of 0.511, specificity of 0.836, NPV of 0.885, and positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.409. The grid plot demonstrated a low incidence of adverse events in the low-risk group (53 of 720 patients [7.4%]) and a comparatively higher incidence in both the intermediate-risk group (32 of 169 patients [18.9%]) and the high-risk group (59 of 190 patients [31.1%]) ( ). Previous studies, including a recent meta-analysis, have also suggested that the high NPV of the PASS supports its utility as a screening tool for risk stratification in pheochromocytoma and PPGL [ ]. Our findings are consistent with these prior reports, indicating that while the predictive accuracy of the PASS system alone may be suboptimal, its high NPV renders it a valuable prognostic grading system. Inter-observer variability of the PASS The PASS is composed of multiple histopathological parameters, many of which lack quantitative or objective criteria. As a result, concerns have been raised regarding inter-observer variability in its application [ , ]. To further assess this issue, the predictive performance of the PASS for adverse events was evaluated across five different hospitals. The AUC for each institution was as follows: hospital A, 0.698; hospital B, 0.513; hospital C, 0.727; hospital D, 0.665; and hospital E, 0.687 ( ). Pairwise DeLong tests revealed statistically significant differences in AUC between hospital A and hospital B, as well as between hospital B and hospital C (p < .05) ( ). These findings indirectly demonstrate inter-observer variability in the application of the PASS score, or at the very least, highlight discrepancies in its predictive performance among different institutions. The distribution of positive cases for each PASS parameter in the adverse event group revealed that nuclear pleomorphism, capsular invasion, and nuclear hyperchromasia were the most frequently observed features ( ). Notably, when the proportion of each PASS parameter was further analyzed across the four participating institutes, substantial variation was observed in several parameters—including capsular invasion and nuclear hyperchromasia ( ). These findings not only identify which parameters are most commonly seen in the adverse event group but also suggest inter-observer variability in PASS parameter assessment among institutions, underscoring the limitation of applying PASS. These findings not only identify which parameters are most commonly seen in the adverse event group but also suggest inter-observer variability in PASS parameter assessment among institutions, underscoring the limitation of applying PASS. Multivariable analysis of PASS parameters and development of the Simple PASS Multivariable logistic regression analysis was conducted on 560 samples with available PASS parameter scoring to evaluate the association between individual PASS parameters and adverse events ( ). Among the PASS parameters, only confluent necrosis, tumor cell spindling, and mitotic figures (>3 per 10 high-power fields [HPF] were statistically significant. Specifically, confluent necrosis was associated with an OR of 3.38 (95% CI, 1.76 to 6.52; p < .001), tumor cell spindling with an OR of 1.89 (95% CI, 1.13 to 3.12; p =.016), and mitotic figures (>3/10 HPF) with an OR of 2.00 (95% CI, 1.10 to 3.58; p = .023). These three parameters were included in the 3-factor Simple PASS, while vascular invasion—despite its marginal significance (OR, 1.64; 95% CI, 0.94 to 2.83; p = .080)—was added to the 4-factor Simple PASS. This decision took into account that other scoring systems, such as GAPP (grading of adrenal pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma) and COPPS (COmposite Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma Prognostic Score), also incorporate vascular invasion as a parameter [ , ]. Based on these odds ratios, the 3-factor Simple PASS was developed by assigning 3 points to confluent necrosis, 2 points to spindling, and 2 points to increased mitotic figures. ROC curve analysis identified an optimal cut-off of 1 point according to the Youden index, indicating that the presence of any single parameter was sufficient to classify a case as high-risk. When high risk was defined as the presence of one or more parameters, subsequent ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.646, sensitivity of 0.519, specificity of 0.740, NPV of 0.837, and PPV of 0.374 ( ). Furthermore, the 4-factor Simple PASS was created by adding vascular invasion, assigned one point, to the original 3-factor model. Using the same optimal cut-off of 1 point, as determined by the Youden index, ROC analysis demonstrated an AUC of 0.701, sensitivity of 0.497, specificity of 0.891, NPV of 0.938, and PPV of 0.374 ( ). Notably, the 4-factor Simple PASS showed improved AUC, specificity, and NPV compared to the original PASS. When comparing the performance of the simplified PASS systems between hospitals A and B, the difference in AUC was less pronounced than that observed with the original PASS in both simplified models ( , ). Importantly, the difference in AUC between the two hospitals for the simplified PASS was not statistically significant (DeLong test p = .658 for the 3-factor model and .465 for the 4-factor model), in contrast to the significant difference observed with the original PASS score (p = .005). These findings suggest that applying the simplified PASS reduces inter-observer variability. DISCUSSION The clinical utility of the PASS system for risk stratification in PPGL has been demonstrated in numerous previous studies, supporting their roles as prognostic indicators for adverse clinical outcomes [ - , , ]. In the present multicenter study, we validated the prognostic impact of PASS using what is, to the best of our knowledge, the largest cohort to date. Our results align with prior research, confirming that PASS is associated with adverse events and RFS. Specifically, multivariable logistic regression analysis in our cohort of 1,518 cases revealed that age and PASS were independent predictors of adverse events, with age per 10 years having an OR of 0.68 (95% CI, 0.60 to 0.76; p < .001) and high-risk PASS scores (≥6) conferring an OR of 4.83 (95% CI, 3.12 to 7.50; p < .001). ROC curve analysis showed that the PASS score had an AUC of 0.673, sensitivity of 0.511, specificity of 0.836, and a notably high NPV of 0.885. These findings are consistent with previous meta-analyses and large-scale studies, which have emphasized the high NPV of the PASS as a screening tool, despite its modest overall discriminative performance [ , - ]. The association between younger age and adverse events may be explained by the fact that adverse events often involve multiplicity, and younger patients are more likely to carry germline mutations and exhibit multiplicity [ - ]. Further studies are warranted to precisely define adverse events using genetic profiles, to distinguish true adverse events from mere multiplicity. Further studies are warranted to precisely define adverse events using genetic profiles, to distinguish true adverse events from mere multiplicity. A major advantage of the PASS system is its simplicity and cost-effectiveness, as it can be assessed solely on histopathological grounds without the need for additional molecular or clinical data [ , ]. However, the PASS system incorporates numerous parameters, many of which lack quantitative definitions, leading to substantial inter-observer variability [ - ]. This issue has been widely recognized in the literature, and our multicenter analysis provides further robust evidence that both the diagnostic validity and interpretative application of the PASS score are subject to considerable variability across institutions. Specifically, diagnostic performance as measured by AUC ranged from 0.513 to 0.727 among the five participating centers, with statistically significant pairwise differences observed in certain comparisons. Furthermore, our detailed exploration of individual PASS parameters demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in their assessment: for instance, capsular invasion and nuclear hyperchromasia showed pronounced discrepancies in the proportion of positive cases among centers. Such inter-institutional differences are likely attributable to variability in pathologists’ interpretation and implementation of the PASS criteria. These results underscore the persistent challenge of inter-observer variability. In response to the limitations of the PASS, several alternative grading systems have been introduced, including the GAPP and other composite models [ - ]. However, each of these systems has its own constraints, such as limited validation, reliance on additional clinical or biochemical data, or continued subjectivity in parameter assessment. Despite these limitations, the PASS remains a valuable screening tool due to its high NPV, and ease of use based solely on histopathology [ ]. To address inter-observer variability and improve the prognostic performance of PASS, we conducted multivariable analysis to identify the parameters most strongly associated with adverse events. Based on these results and previous studies, confluent necrosis, tumor cell spindling, and increased mitotic figures (>3/10 HPF) were incorporated into a 3-factor simplified PASS scoring system, while vascular invasion was additionally included to develop a 4-factor simplified PASS. Notably, the 4-factor model—where single presence of vascular invasion, necrosis, spindling and increased mitosis can be assigned as high-risk group—demonstrated improved AUC (0.701), specificity (0.891), and NPV (0.938) compared to the original PASS score, despite the reduced number of parameters. Furthermore, when comparing the performance of both simplified PASS systems between hospitals A and B, the difference in AUC was not statistically significant, suggesting reduced inter-observer variability relative to the original PASS system. This study has several limitations. First, we did not review pathological slides or revise the initially diagnosed PASS to avoid retrospective bias, as the main goal of this study was to evaluate how well the PASS system performs in real-world practice with respect to diagnostic accuracy and inter-observer variability. During data collection, we realized that the absence of a refined consensus on the definitions of each parameter might have contributed to inter-observer variability, underscoring the high demand for precise and standardized definitions of each factor. As a multicenter retrospective analysis, the completeness and consistency of data collection may be suboptimal. While the relationship between PASS score and adverse events was the primary focus, survival data and detailed PASS parameter information was limited, resulting in smaller sample sizes (n = 560) for some analyses. Furthermore, we did not directly assess inter-observer agreement by having multiple pathologists independently review the same slides; rather, we inferred variability indirectly by comparing AUCs for adverse event prediction across institutions. Future studies should incorporate direct inter-observer concordance assessments to more precisely quantify variability. Another limitation concerns the definition of adverse events. Given that PPGL can arise anywhere along the paraganglionic system, distinguishing between multifocality, metastasis, and recurrence can be challenging, and these categories may overlap biologically [ , ]. We included multifocal tumors as adverse events but recognize that their biological behavior may differ from truly metastatic or recurrent tumors, potentially diminishing the predictive power of the PASS [ , ]. Additionally, previous studies suggest patients with germline mutations are more prone to multifocal PPGL, and immunohistochemistry (IHC) for S-100 and SOX-10 can be used to distinguish metastasis from multifocal tumors [ , - ]. Taken together, future research should incorporate genetic data and additional IHC study to distinguish multifocal cases from metastasis and refine the definition of adverse events accordingly. chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Primary aldosteronism is a common, under-recognized cause of secondary hypertension and is present in approximately 5–10% of all hypertensive patients [ , ]. Compared with essential hypertension (EHT), primary aldosteronism is associated with greater cardiovascular risk and target-organ damage, partly attributed to mineralocorticoid receptor–mediated inflammation, fibrosis, and oxidative stress beyond blood-pressure load [ , ]. Cardiac remodeling is a salient downstream consequence of renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) dysregulation. Patients with primary aldosteronism more often show left ventricular hypertrophy and myocardial fibrosis, often out of proportion to blood pressure; targeted treatment can partially reverse these changes [ ]. Left ventricular mass index (LVMI) is a robust marker of structural remodeling, whereas excess LVMI (eLVMI) quantifies left ventricular mass beyond that predicted by hemodynamic load, capturing maladaptive remodeling associated with adverse outcomes [ ]. Aging strongly shapes morbidity and mortality, but chronological age incompletely reflects inter-individual biological aging [ ]. The Gompertz law–based biological age (GOLD BioAge) model, derived from routine clinical biomarkers – offers a practical estimate of biological age [ ]; GOLD BioAgeDiff (BioAge–chronological age) predicts morbidity and mortality in general populations [ ]. Whether RAAS perturbations in primary aldosteronism are associated with accelerated biological aging, and whether this aging burden tracks cardiac structural remodeling remain unclear [ , ]. We hypothesized that elevated plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC), suppressed plasma renin activity (PRA), and a higher aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) are associated with higher GOLD BioAgeDiff, which correlates with greater LVMI and eLVMI. METHODS Data sources This study is part of the Study on Primary Aldosteronism in Nanchang (NPAS), which was registered at Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2200057297; https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=133752 ). NPAS is an inpatient hypertension screening cohort established in 2017. The protocol was approved by the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University (approval number: 2022-05) and complied with the Declaration of Helsinki; prospective participants provided written informed consent, and retrospective data were de-identified before analysis. Study design, setting, and participants We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of hypertensive inpatients undergoing standardized evaluation for secondary hypertension at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University (Nanchang, China). Clinical information from these routine screenings was curated into the NPAS database. Participants were classified into two groups based on their final diagnosis. The primary aldosteronism group consisted of consecutive patients diagnosed with primary aldosteronism and hospitalized between October 2017 and November 2022. The EHT group was drawn from patients hospitalized for screening between January 2019 and June 2019, in whom secondary causes were excluded. For the primary analysis, patients were excluded if they had missing data on key variables [age, serum creatinine (Scr), plasma glucose (Glu), mean corpuscular volume (MCV), red cell distribution width (RDW), serum albumin (Alb), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), lymphocyte percentage (Lym%), white blood cell count (WBC), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), ARR, or postcaptopril PAC)], had a diagnosis of secondary hypertension other than primary aldosteronism, such as renovascular hypertension due to renal artery stenosis, renal hypertension due to renal parenchymal disease, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea, and gestational hypertension. or presented with extreme GOLD BioAge values (1.5 × interquartile range). For echocardiographic analyses, we additionally excluded patients without echocardiography. Diagnosis of primary aldosteronism The diagnosis of primary aldosteronism was made according to the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline [ ], as previously described in our published work [ ]. Briefly, prior to admission, Patients stopped ARR-interfering medications or switched to verapamil and/or terazosin for 2–4 weeks. An ARR greater than 30 [(ng/dl)/(ng/ml/h)] prompted confirmatory testing (captopril challenge or saline infusion) to diagnose primary aldosteronism. Diagnosis of essential hypertension EHT was defined by office SBP at least 140 mmHg and/or DBP 90 mmHg on repeated inpatient measurements or a documented hypertension history with current treatment [ ], after excluding secondary causes through standardized work-up. Primary aldosteronism was excluded by ARR 30 or less under standardized medication preparation or by negative confirmatory testing when ARR was elevated [ ]. In addition, all secondary causes of hypertension were excluded through the standardized inpatient work-up as described above. Exclusion relied on history and physical examination, routine laboratory testing including renal function and urinalysis, endocrine assays when appropriate, and imaging or functional testing as clinically indicated. The final EHT diagnosis was determined by the treating physicians. PRA was derived from angiotensin I generation during incubation (4 versus 37 °C), and ARR was calculated as PAC/PRA. PRA was derived from angiotensin I generation during incubation (4 versus 37 °C), and ARR was calculated as PAC/PRA. For the primary aldosteronism screening test, samples for PAC and PRA were collected after subjects had been in a sitting or standing position for at least 2 h. Clinical data and comorbidity information were obtained from the electronic medical record system and the hospital's central testing laboratory, including sex, age, height, weight, duration of hypertension, SBP, DBP, smoking history, alcohol consumption, MCV, RDW, Alb, ALP, Glu, Lym%, WBC, GGT, serum potassium, serum sodium, total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), Scr, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Smoking history was defined as smoking more than one cigarette per day, at least 1 year, or 18 packs per year. Alcohol drinking history was defined as on average, drinking alcohol at least two times a week for more than 1 year. Comorbidities were identified based on discharge diagnoses determined by specialist physicians in accordance with standard clinical guidelines. Outcome The primary outcome was GOLD BioAgeDiff, defined as the difference between the GOLD BioAge and chronological age. GOLD BioAge was calculated using the GOLD BioAge model [ ]: GOLD BioAge = chronological age+ ∑(β i × Biomarker i ) + β 0 (β 0 = −53.6287), where biomarkers were Scr, Glu, MCV, RDW, Alb, ALP, Lym%, WBC, and GGT. GOLD BioAgeDiff was defined as GOLD BioAge − chronological age. The secondary outcomes were LVMI and eLVMI. Doppler echocardiography was used to evaluate the cardiac structure as described previously [ ]. Echocardiography was performed by experienced sonographers blinded to diagnosis using standardized measurements. Two-dimensional and two-dimensionally guided M-mode images were recorded from standardized views. Left ventricular internal diameter in diastole (LVIDd), posterior wall thickness in diastole (PWTd), and interventricular septal thickness in diastole (SWTd) were measured and incorporated into the Devereux-modified formula to estimate left ventricular (LV) mass. LV mass was calculated by the formula: LV mass = 0.8 × {1.04[(LVIDd + PWTd + SWTd) 3 – (LVIDd) 3 ]} + 0.6 (g) [ ]. LVMI was calculated by dividing LV mass by body surface area (BSA). The body surface area was calculated as follow: BSA (m 2 ) = 0.0061 × height (cm) + 0.0128 × weight (kg) − 0.1529 [ ]. Stroke volume was derived using the Teichholz method [ ]. Stroke work was estimated as SBP (mmHg) × stroke volume (ml) × 0.0144 (g m), as previously described [ ]. As simultaneous SBP measurement immediately after echocardiography was not routinely available, we used admission SBP recorded within 48 h of the echocardiographic examination as a surrogate for systolic loading conditions. The predicted LVM was estimated by the equation derived previously: predicted LVM = 55.37 + 6.64 × height (m 2.7 ) + 0.64 × stroke work − 18.07 × sex (where sex was coded as male = 1 and female = 2) [ , ]. Predicted LVMI was then calculated as predicted LVM/BSA. The eLVMI was defined as measured LVMI − predicted LVMI [ ]. Statistical analysis Variables with at least 20% missing data were excluded from the analysis. For those with 20% or less missing values, missing data were imputed using multiple imputation, implemented through the mice package in R. Clinical characteristics were compared between patients with primary aldosteronism and those with EHT. Normally distributed data are presented as mean (SD) and compared using the Student's t test; nonnormally distributed data are summarized as median [IQR] and compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Categorical variables are described as counts (percentages) and compared using the χ 2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. ARR was log-transformed due to skewed distributions. Multivariable linear regression models were constructed for the primary analysis to evaluate the association of RAAS measures with GOLD BioAgeDiff, and for the secondary analysis to examine the relationship between GOLD BioAgeDiff and LVMI/eLVMI. Covariates were likewise selected a priori based upon clinical knowledge, previous literature, and data availability. For the primary analysis: Model 1 was unadjusted. Model 2 adjusted for sex, age, and BMI. Model 3 further adjusted for SBP, DBP, serum potassium, TC, triglycerides, HDL-C, LDL-C, cardiac insufficiency, peripheral vascular disease, coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, stroke, smoking, alcohol, and hypertension duration. For the secondary analysis: Model 1 was unadjusted. Model 2 adjusted for the full set of covariates used in primary Model 3. Model 3 was additionally adjusted for PAC, PRA, and log-ARR. Given the significant interaction between disease subtype (primary aldosteronism versus EHT) and ARR, subgroup analyses were restricted to the primary aldosteronism population. Mediation analyses were performed using nonparametric bootstrapping with 1000 iterations to examine whether GOLD BioAgeDiff mediates the association between ARR and eLVMI. These models were adjusted for sex, age, BMI, smoking, and alcohol. To compare mediation effects between primary aldosteronism and EHT, a bootstrap-based difference test with 5000 samples was conducted; significance was inferred if the 95% confidence interval (CI) of the average causal mediation effect (ACME) difference (Δ = ACME_PA − ACME_EHT) excluded zero [ ]. RESULTS Characteristics of the study population From October 2017 to November 2022, a total of 1053 patients diagnosed with primary aldosteronism were initially screened. In addition, 616 patients with EHT without primary aldosteronism, enrolled between January 2019 and June 2019, were included as a comparison group. After excluding 337 patients with missing data, 117 with concomitant secondary hypertension other than primary aldosteronism, and 14 with extreme GOLD BioAge values, 1201 patients were eligible for primary analysis, including 785 patients with primary aldosteronism and 416 patients with EHT. For the secondary analysis focused on echocardiographic outcomes, a further 92 patients without available echocardiography were excluded, yielding 1109 participants including 717 patients with primary aldosteronism and 392 patients with EHT (Fig. ). Among the 1201 patients included in the primary analysis, the mean age was 49.4 (11.0) years and 687 (57.2%) were men. The mean GOLD BioAge was 57 (13) years, and the mean GOLD BioAgeDiff was 7.6 (4.7) years. Compared with EHT, primary aldosteronism patients had the expected RAAS profile (lower PRA and higher PAC/ARR), were older with longer hypertension duration, and differed in electrolytes, lipids, and comorbidity patterns (Table ). Association between aldosterone, renin, and aldosterone-to-renin ratio and Gompertz law–based biological age difference In the overall cohort, RAAS indices were positively associated with GOLD BioAgeDiff (Table ). PhenoAge is an epigenetic biomarker calculated by weighting DNA methylation levels at 513 CpG sites [ ]. Primary aldosteronism features autonomous aldosterone excess with renin suppression, leading to chronic mineralocorticoid receptor activation [ ]. Mineralocorticoid receptor activation promotes oxidative stress and sterile inflammation, pro-fibrotic/vascular remodeling, and endothelial dysfunction with microvascular impairment across organs [ ]. Persistent mineralocorticoid receptor activation may induce mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species generation, amplifying oxidative stress and inflammation [ ]. This cascade may also intersect with aging biology through Klotho-related pathways [ ]. Clinically, primary aldosteronism is associated with greater arterial stiffness and vascular aging than EHT, supporting blood pressure–independent pro-aging vascular effects of aldosterone [ ]. Furthermore, higher aldosterone exposure has also been associated with shorter leukocyte telomere length, consistent with aldosterone-related cellular senescence [ ]. Because these pathways affect inflammation, metabolism, and organ function, domains captured by the biomarkers in GOLD BioAge, mineralocorticoid receptor-mediated injury may manifest as a higher multisystem ‘aging burden’. This mechanism elucidates the phenomenon observed in our study: after fully adjusting for potential confounding factors, aldosterone-related indices remained independently and positively correlated with GOLD BioAgeDiff. Previous studies have provided strong evidence that accelerated biological aging aligns with structural target-organ damage, including cardiac remodeling. Recently, using UK Biobank data, Mao et al. showed that biological age acceleration, calculated via the the Klemera–Doubal and PhenoAge algorithms [ , ], was associated with adverse cardiac structure and function and a higher risk of incident heart failure; their Mendelian randomization analyses further suggested a potential causal contribution to cardiac remodeling [ ]. Higher ARR has been associated with arterial stiffness, LV hypertrophy, and atrial enlargement, partly independent of blood-pressure load [ ]. eLVMI represents LV mass beyond that predicted by body size and hemodynamic load, and may better reflect maladaptive, nonhemodynamic remodeling [ ]. In primary aldosteronism, GOLD BioAgeDiff was independently associated with LVMI and eLVMI, aligning with Mao et al. Mediation analyses further indicated that GOLD BioAgeDiff statistically accounted for part of the log-ARR–eLVMI association, though establishing causality and temporality requires longitudinal and interventional validation. In the subgroup analyses stratified by clinical characteristics, a nominal interaction was observed regarding diabetes status ( P for interaction = 0.036). The positive association between log-ARR and GOLD BioAgeDiff was prominent in participants without diabetes but was not statistically significant in those with concomitant diabetes. Diabetes is a strong driver of oxidative stress and inflammation and may produce a ‘ceiling effect’ that attenuates additional aldosterone-related aging signals [ , ]. Antidiabetic therapies such as metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors may also exert cardiometabolic benefits that modify RAAS-related injury signals [ – ]. Because subgroup analyses were exploratory and the diabetic subgroup was smaller, this interaction should be considered hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation. Methodologically, we used the complete GOLD BioAge model rather than Light BioAge because C-reactive protein required for the simplified model was not routinely measured [ ]. Additionally, the complete model includes immune cell, erythrocyte, and hepatobiliary indices that may better capture primary aldosteronism-related multisystem attrition [ , – ]. Because GOLD BioAge was developed in Western general populations, calibration in Chinese primary aldosteronism cohorts warrants evaluation. Nevertheless, applying the same algorithm across groups supports internal comparisons even if absolute biological age values shift systematically. GOLD BioAgeDiff is readily computed from routine laboratory indices and may serve as a quantitative phenotype of multisystem burden in primary aldosteronism. Its association with LVMI/eLVMI suggests potential utility for refined risk stratification and prioritizing cardiac assessment. chunks.content: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) syndrome is a rare inherited tumor syndrome caused by germline pathogenic variants in the MEN1 gene coding the menin protein [ ]. Loss of heterozygosity and inactivation of both alleles of this gene predispose to MEN1 syndrome [ , ]. Menin is a scaffold chromatic adaptor protein, which interacts with various cellular proteins, including different nuclear receptors, epigenetic and cellular transcription factors, which are involved in gene regulation, DNA repair, and signaling transmission [ , ]. Menin has contradictory effects both as an oncogenic cofactor and as a tumor suppressor, depending on tissue type and cellular context [ , ]. In MEN1, abnormal structures and functions of menin are assumed to cause several changes in cellular functions and predispose to tumorigenesis [ ]. Clinically, MEN1 syndrome is typically characterized by an increased risk of neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) [ , , ]. These include parathyroid (pHPT), pituitary (PitNET), and pancreatic NETs (PNET), and less often other gastro-intestinal NETs. Other well-known but rarer tumors are thymic (TNET) and bronchopulmonary NETs [ , ]. Adrenal tumors (AdrT) are also present in more than 20% of MEN1 patients [ ]. In addition to neuroendocrine tumors, MEN1 syndrome has also been associated with more than 20 different neoplasms [ , ]. Several studies have reported an increased prevalence of breast cancer (BC) in MEN1 compared to the general population [ , ]. There are also reports of possible associations between MEN1 and thyroid [ , ] and urogenital cancers [ , ]. The aims of this study were (1) to evaluate the prevalence of BC, thyroid, and renal cancers (RC) previously reported in the literature to be associated with MEN1 in a registry-based retrospective Finnish MEN1 cohort and (2) to compare the findings with a representative local control population. Materials and methods Study population The data were collected at the Department of Endocrinology at Oulu University Hospital between November 1982 and December 2023 and all patients diagnosed with MEN1 during that period were included in the data collection ( n = 113, 45.1% males). The criteria for MEN1 diagnosis were applied according to previous guidelines [ , ]. All but one of our patients had a genetically confirmed diagnosis of MEN1. The patient without genetic MEN1 confirmation had pHPT and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome caused by a gastrinoma, meaning she had a clinical MEN1. The Oulu Project Elucidating Risk of Atherosclerosis (OPERA) was utilized as a control population. OPERA is an epidemiological cohort study originally designed for addressing cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors and clinical endpoints. Subjects ( n = 1045, 50% hypertensives, 50% males, age 40-62 years) were middle-aged hypertensives and their age- and sex-matched controls who were randomly selected between 1990-1993 from the local area, as previously described in detail [ ]. At baseline, participants were interviewed, examined, and tested in the University of Oulu research laboratory. Mortality and hospital events of the population have since been followed and the project is ongoing, with the latest major data collection in 2014. A flowchart presenting the study setup, and the analyses carried out is presented in the supplementary data (Fig. S1) [ ]. The study protocol was approved by the medical ethics committee of the North Ostrobothnia Hospital District and board reviews at Oulu University Hospital. Genetic studies of the MEN1 gene in the patients have been conducted as part of routine clinical work and counseling process. All participants of the OPERA cohort gave written informed consent. The Declaration of Helsinki 1975 was adhered to during the study. Clinical data and outcome classification Patient data, including clinical information such as sex, age at diagnosis of MEN1, family history, characteristics of tumors, their treatment, and outcomes, were obtained from both electronic medical records and clinical charts. Data on MEN1 patients were collected until the end of 2024, and on the control population until the end of 2014. The outcome “breast cancer” included all recorded BCs, including lobular carcinomas and ductal carcinomas. The outcome “thyroid cancer” included all recorded thyroid carcinomas. In both cohorts, all recorded thyroid cancers were papillary thyroid carcinomas (PTC). The outcome “renal cancer” (RC) included all recorded renal cell carcinomas (RCCs), including clear cell (CCRCC) and papillary (PRCC) carcinomas. Kaplan–Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate the associations of MEN1 syndrome with the outcomes. A total of 33 women (3.2%) in the OPERA control cohort were diagnosed with BC compared to the 7 women in the MEN1 cohort (6.2%). In the OPERA control cohort, only 11 patients (1.1%) were diagnosed with PTC, a significantly lower prevalence than in the MEN1 cohort (6.2%) ( P < .001, Table S5) [ ]. The average age of PTC diagnosis in the control cohort was 49.6 years compared to 44.4 years in the MEN1 patients (Table S5) [ ]. In a crude Cox regression model, the HR for PTC in all MEN1 patients was 9.37 (3.59-24.41) ( ), 12.87 (3.70-45.03) in female MEN1 patients (Figure S2B) [ ], and 5.74 (1.14-28.8) in male MEN1 patients (Fig. S3A) [ ], respectively. Two BC MEN1 women carried missense variants, one had c.1252G > A (p.Asp418Asn) on exon 9 and the other c.466G > C on exon 3 (p.Gly156Arg). The prevalent variant is 1 of our 2 founder mutations in Northern Finland [ ]. All these variants are supposed to result in a structurally and functionally altered menin protein. Curiously, there were no women with BC in our other large pedigree of MEN1 patients with the pathogenic variant c.1546dup in exon 10. Genetic testing is the only definitive confirmatory test for the diagnosis of MEN1. The traditional consensus has been that there are no genotype–phenotype correlations in genetically confirmed MEN1 [ ]. This conclusion has recently been challenged [ ], and our data suggest that in the case of some non-neuroendocrine cancers in MEN1, such correlations require further studies. Previous studies have reported BC with a mean age of diagnosis ranging from 48 to 56 years (median age of 45 years) in women with MEN1 [ , , , ]. In our study, the mean age of diagnosis of BC was 50 years in women with MEN1, lower than in female OPERA controls (62 years) or in the average Finnish female population (65 years) (FCR). BC was diagnosed in 11.5% of our MEN1 women (on average after 58 patient-years of follow-up) compared to 6.3% in female OPERA controls (on average after 73 patient-years of follow-up) and 8.3% to 11.2% in female population statistics from the Finnish Cancer Registry (70-80-year-old females) (FRC). The actual lifetime point prevalence in Finnish women to develop BC is 13.4% (FCR), and the incidence of BC in Finland has more than doubled from 1980 to the year 2020. In recent MEN1 cohorts, BC has been reported in 1.7% to 4.2% of MEN1 female patients [ , , ]. When compared to our local OPERA control cohort, the risk for developing BC in our MEN1 women was 3.79 (1.66-8.60), slightly higher than the previously reported risks from other cohorts, ranging from 2.31 to 2.83 [ ]. Our data suggest that BC can manifest in MEN1 women significantly earlier than in the average population, but data on the overall point prevalence of BC in MEN1 is currently lacking. The MEN1 gene codes for the protein is menin [ ]. It is widely expressed in various tissues and mostly expressed in the cell nucleus [ ]. It is a scaffold nuclear protein, which has interactions with more than 50 different nuclear proteins and functions through such interacting partners, especially with those which regulate and control transcription, epigenetic regulation, chromatin modifiers, DNA repair proteins, and cell signaling proteins [ ]. In typical NETs in MEN1, loss of menin and its tumor suppressive effects is thought to lead to the disruption of antiproliferative gene expression programs and to development of tumors [ , ]. In certain sporadic solid tumors such as BC, previous studies have found that menin can also have a pro-oncogenic effect and could be involved in BC pathogenesis [ , ]. Moreover, menin inhibitors have been tested as an adjunct to BC treatment [ , ]. Menin binds and is a coactivator for the nuclear protein estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) and regulates the expression of the gene ESR1 coding ERα, which are important drivers for BC tumorigenesis [ , ]. Although clinical and experimental data suggest an association of MEN1 syndrome and BC, the causal relationship remains uncertain [ , ]. Breast carcinogenesis is a multistep and complex process involving the accumulation of genetic alterations and is influenced by various environmental and hormonal risk factors [ , , , ]. In a Dutch study of MEN1 patients, various BC risk factors were analyzed and the findings indicated that the increased BC risk in MEN1 carriers was not related to other known BC risk factors or familial cancer history [ ]. About 5% to 10% of BC patients have inherited predisposition due to germline mutations of various BC risk genes [ ]. However, there are only 2 previous reports where BC risk genes have been studied in MEN1 patients [ , ]. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the only one in which known BC risk genes have been reported in MEN1 BC women. We analyzed an extensive panel of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants of BC genes available in 6 out of 7 of our BC patients. We did not find highly penetrant BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene variants on them, which have been previously noted in case reports with simultaneous mutations in both MEN1 and BRCA2 or MEN1 and BRCA1 genes [ , ]. Also, other pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in established BC genes were excluded in our patients. Previous large studies on genetic predisposition to BC have been unable to identify the MEN1 gene as a significant susceptibility gene in women with sporadic BC [ , ] or in women with hereditary BC [ , ], but MEN1 somatic mutations seem to have a driver role in women with metastatic BC [ ]. In conclusion, menin seems to have a role in BC tumorigenesis, but in BC of MEN1 patients, the pathogenesis is uncertain, and it is thought that menin alone is not sufficient for BC development [ ]. A higher prevalence of PTC was observed in our MEN1 patients (6.2%) compared to the OPERA controls (1.1%). Based on the Finnish Cancer Registry, the risk of developing PTC before the age of 70-80 years is 0.53% to 0.65% in the general population (FCR), indicating a similar prevalence as in our OPERA control cohort. The HR for PTC in our MEN1 patients was 9.37 (3.59-24.41) compared to the OPERA control cohort. Thus, our data suggest a higher prevalence of PTC in MEN1 patients compared to the general population. Although there are reports of a possible association between MEN1 and thyroid cancer [ , ], this relationship is thought to be incidental, possibly at least partially related to increased use of ultrasound examination [ ], and no loss of heterozygosity of the MEN1 locus has been observed in PTC tumor tissue in MEN1 patients [ ]. It has been concluded that there is no robust evidence from in vitro , animal, or human studies linking germline mutation of the MEN1 gene with the development of PTC [ , ]. Although we report an increased prevalence of PTC in MEN1 patients, this finding may be due to surveillance bias, and there is currently insufficient data to support a causal association between MEN1, and the occurrence of PTC and further studies are warranted. Although our data are consistent with current knowledge, several validity issues must be considered. We lack reliable information on socioeconomic and behavioral factors such as smoking and occupation, established cancer risk factors, and details on how certain cancers were initially diagnosed. It can also not be excluded that an unknown genetic factor closely linked to MEN1 could contribute to the increased risk of cancer types observed in our MEN1 patients. Our OPERA control cohort does not directly represent a general population cohort, is not designed for cancer incidence evaluation, and is not age-matched or matched for key clinical breast cancer (BC) risk factors relative to our study population. Because the OPERA cohort was not originally intended as a control cohort for MEN1, information on several important risk factors for our main outcomes is missing, and therefore, these factors could not be included in our regression models. For BC, however, the most important risk factors according to the World Health Organization are female sex and age. Both are accounted for in our models, as Cox regression inherently adjusts for age, and we performed separate analyses for men and women. In addition, we excluded the possibility of known high-risk BC genes such as BRCA1/2 in our MEN1 patients with BC, thereby addressing another major category of BC risk factors. Nevertheless, we lack information on reproductive history and postmenopausal hormone therapy in both the OPERA controls and the MEN1 cohort, meaning that residual confounding may partly explain the magnitude of the observed hazard ratios. The National Breast Cancer Screening Program in Finland was launched in 1987 for women aged 50 to 59 years and expanded to include women aged 50 to 69 years in 2007. Invitation coverage increased among women over 60 years of age until 2016, reaching over 95% in 2014. Thus, although the data collection periods for the OPERA cohort and the MEN1 cohort differ slightly, BC screening practices were largely comparable between the 2 groups. Moreover, the OPERA control cohort is slightly older and has a longer follow-up period than our MEN1 cohort, suggesting that if anything, the OPERA cohort should have a higher cancer prevalence than an age-matched control cohort. The OPERA population is also local, and the study period (1990s-2000s) aligns well with the time frame of most MEN1 patient data. Finally, our findings are further supported by comparisons with population-based data from the Finnish Cancer Registry. The demographics of our MEN1 cohort are similar to those reported in three large MEN1 cohorts from the Netherlands, Italy, and France [ , , ]. In summary, in this retrospective study, the risk of BC, PTC, and RC was higher in MEN1 patients compared with controls. Among women with MEN1 in whom other germline mutations in BC risk genes had been excluded, BC was diagnosed, on average, more than a decade earlier than in the control subjects. Our findings support the original Dutch and subsequent recommendations to initiate BC screening in women with MEN1 at the age of 40 years [ , ].
